claims.text: Controlled heat treatment promotes diffusion-driven partitioning of Al and, when present, Ti.
Al/Ti partitioning nucleates γ′-like precipitates.
The γ′-like precipitates are coherent and are stabilized by the partitioning process.
Phase separation mediates the interplay between solid-solution strengthening and precipitate strengthening.
Precipitation-mediated phase separation governs phase stability in Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni alloys.
This precipitation mechanism enables retention of high-temperature strength, environmental resistance, radiation tolerance, and cryogenic toughness.
The solution-annealed baseline is a homogeneous single-phase solid solution lacking a precipitate microstructure.
Aging at 750°C for varying durations induces precipitate nucleation and growth.
Precipitate volume fraction, size distribution, and composition are structural mediators of the resulting properties.
The γ′-like precipitates are enriched in Al and Ti relative to the matrix.
Diffusion-controlled elemental partitioning during aging causes precipitate nucleation and coherent growth.
The precipitates strengthen the alloy through interfacial strengthening and dislocation pinning.
The precipitates stabilize the phase structure against coarsening.
Relative to the solution-annealed baseline, aging produces a significant, well-dispersed precipitate population.
Relative to the solution-annealed baseline, aging increases high-temperature yield strength.
Relative to the solution-annealed baseline, aging preserves or enhances cryogenic toughness.
Relative to the solution-annealed baseline, aging improves resistance to environmental degradation.
The proposed precipitate structure maintains radiation resistance.
The proposed mechanism may not apply after changes in alloying elements or under non-isothermal processing.

Failure to obtain statistically significant Al/Ti-partitioned precipitation together with failure to improve the targeted properties relative to the solution-annealed control would falsify the hypothesis.
